chunks: Which SoC blocks use the most power. The question: Which blocks of the SoC consume the most power?
It depends on what the chip is doing. Under heavy work, the biggest users are the compute blocks: the CPU cores, the graphics block (GPU) and, for AI work, the neural engine.
Moving data to and from main memory comes close behind. When the chip sits idle, a small leftover current called leakage matters most.
Designers save power by keeping unused blocks off.
Picture a workshop. The big machines use the most electricity while they run. Trips to a distant warehouse for materials also burn real fuel, often more than the work itself.
At night, nothing runs, but a few lights stay on, and that trickle adds up. Compute is the machines, memory trips are the warehouse runs, and leakage is the lights.
The best savings come from switching off whatever you are not using.
At 3 gigahertz both strategies use 0. 9 volts and 2. 9 watts. Dropping to 1 gigahertz with fixed voltage gives only a linear saving (0.
97 watts) but with DVFS the voltage also falls and power drops to 0. 59 watts. Energy per operation tells the same story: at 1 gigahertz the DVFS point uses (0. 7 over 0.
9) squared equals 60 % of the energy per cycle. Voltage cannot fall below a minimum where logic still meets timing, which is why DVFS curves flatten at low frequencies.
Dynamic power: power spent while circuits switch, because each switch fills or empties wires with charge.
It is about C V squared f : capacitance (how much charge the wiring holds per volt), voltage squared, and clock frequency.
Leakage: a small current that flows through transistors (the chip's tiny switches) even when nothing switches.
DVFS: lowering voltage and frequency together when less speed is needed. Clock gating: stopping the clock to an idle block so it does not switch.
Power gating: cutting the supply to an idle block, which also removes its leakage. Workload: the job the chip is doing right now.
Take a CPU cluster with an effective switched capacitance (the total capacitance that flips each cycle) of 1. 2 nanofarads. At 0. 9 volts and 2. 5 gigahertz, P equals 1.
2 times 10 to the -9 times 0. 9 squared times 2. 5 times 10 to the 9 about 2. 43 watts. Drop to 0. 7 volts and 1. 5 gigahertz. Now P about 0. 88 watts.
Frequency fell to 60%, but power fell to 36%, because voltage counts squared. That is the whole idea.
"Under load it's the compute blocks, the CPU cluster and GPU, and NPU if it's running, followed closely by the memory subsystem, because moving data from DRAM costs far more than computing on it.
Dynamic power goes as alpha C V squared f, so high-voltage, high-frequency blocks dominate; at idle, leakage in SRAM and powered domains does.
Designers manage it with clock and power gating, DVFS, heterogeneous cores and fixed-function engines."
